The Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to 229 individuals as of 2025.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The first prize in physics was [awarded in 1901](/wiki/1901_Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "1901 Nobel Prize in Physics") to [Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen](/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen "Wilhelm Röntgen"), of Germany, who received 150,782 [SEK](/wiki/Swedish_krona "Swedish krona"). [John Bardeen](/wiki/John_Bardeen "John Bardeen") is the only laureate to win the prize twice—in 1956 and 1972.

[William Lawrence Bragg](/wiki/Lawrence_Bragg "Lawrence Bragg") was the youngest Nobel laureate in physics; he won the prize in 1915 at the age of 25. He was also the youngest laureate for any Nobel prize until 2014 (when [Malala Yousafzai](/wiki/Malala_Yousafzai "Malala Yousafzai") won the Nobel Peace Prize at the age of 17).[[6]](#cite_note-6) The oldest Nobel Prize laureate in physics was [Arthur Ashkin](/wiki/Arthur_Ashkin "Arthur Ashkin") who was 96 years old when he was awarded the prize in 2018.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Only five women have won the prize: [Marie Curie](/wiki/Marie_Curie "Marie Curie") (1903), [Maria Goeppert-Mayer](/wiki/Maria_Goeppert-Mayer "Maria Goeppert-Mayer") (1963), [Donna Strickland](/wiki/Donna_Strickland "Donna Strickland") (2018), [Andrea Ghez](/wiki/Andrea_Ghez "Andrea Ghez") (2020), and [Anne L'Huillier](/wiki/Anne_L%27Huillier "Anne L'Huillier") (2023).[[8]](#cite_note-8) Before L'Huillier, each woman only ever received a quarter share of the prize, although Marie Curie did receive an [unshared Nobel prize in chemistry in 1911](/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Chemistry "List of Nobel laureates in Chemistry"). In 2023, L'Huillier received a one-third share.

CIThe [Cinerama](/wiki/Cinerama "Cinerama") figures represent gross amounts. Since the Cinerama corporation owned the theaters there were no rental fees for the films, meaning the studio received 100% of the box-office gross, unlike the case with most other films where the distributor typically receives less than half the gross. Since *Variety* at the time ranked films by their U.S. and Canadian rental, they constructed a hypothetical rental figure for the Cinerama films to provide a basis for comparison to other films in their chart: in the case of *This Is Cinerama*, the $50 million worldwide gross was reconfigured as a $12.5 million U.S. rental gross; this is exactly 25% of the amount reported by Cinerama, so *Variety*'s formula seemingly halved the gross to obtain an estimate for the U.S. share, and halved it again to simulate a rental fee.[[65]](#cite_note-383) All five Cinerama features collectively generated $120 million in worldwide box office receipts.[[66]](#cite_note-384)

GS*Variety* put the worldwide rental for *The Greatest Show on Earth* at around $18.35 million (with $12.8 million coming from the United States[[56]](#cite_note-Finler358-374)) a year after its release; however, Birchard puts its earnings at just over $15 million up to 1962. It is likely that Birchard's figure is just the North American gross rental, and includes revenue from the 1954 and 1960 reissues.

SWThe "first run" *Star Wars* grosses do not include revenue from the 1997 special-edition releases; however, the figure does include revenue from the re-releases prior to the [special editions](/wiki/Star_Wars_(film)#Special_Edition "Star Wars (film)").

Stanford's endowment includes real estate and other investments valued at $36.5 billion as of August 2023,[[130]](#cite_note-133) and is one of the four [largest academic endowments](/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment "List of colleges and universities in the United States by endowment") in the United States.[[131]](#cite_note-134) The endowment consists of $29.9 billion in a merged pool of assets and $6.6 billion of real estate near the main campus. Stanford is the largest landowner in the Silicon Valley[[132]](#cite_note-135) Payouts from the endowment covered approximately 22% of university expenses in the 2023 fiscal year.[[133]](#cite_note-2023FinRep-136)

Since inception, the university has been the beneficiary of large donations. The endowment began in 1885, six years before the opening of the university, when Leland Stanford and his wife Jane conveyed approximately $20 million to the university.[[134]](#cite_note-137) The university's pioneering of technology intellectual property transfer created both direct investments and enabled a unique pipeline of mega-donors[[135]](#cite_note-138) including from alumni-founded companies with [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") ([Sergey Brin](/wiki/Sergey_Brin "Sergey Brin") and [Larry Page](/wiki/Larry_Page "Larry Page")), [Nike](/wiki/Nike,_Inc. For information on Christie's book originally titled *Ten Little Niggers*, see [And Then There Were None](/wiki/And_Then_There_Were_None "And Then There Were None").

Christie included stereotyped descriptions of characters in her work, especially before 1945 (when such attitudes were more commonly expressed publicly), particularly in regard to Italians, Jews, and non-Europeans.[[8]](#cite_note-Morgan1984-8): 264–66 For example, she described "men of [Hebraic](/wiki/Hebrews "Hebrews") extraction, sallow men with hooked noses, wearing rather flamboyant jewellery" in the short story "The Soul of the Croupier" from the collection *[The Mysterious Mr Quin](/wiki/The_Mysterious_Mr_Quin "The Mysterious Mr Quin")*. In 1947, the [Anti-Defamation League](/wiki/Anti-Defamation_League "Anti-Defamation League") in the US sent an official letter of complaint to Christie's American publishers, [Dodd, Mead and Company](/wiki/Dodd,_Mead_and_Company "Dodd, Mead and Company"), regarding perceived [antisemitism](/wiki/Antisemitism "Antisemitism") in her works. Christie's British literary agent later wrote to her US representative, authorising American publishers to "omit the word 'Jew' when it refers to an unpleasant character in future books."[[18]](#cite_note-thompson-19): 386

In *[The Hollow](/wiki/The_Hollow "The Hollow")*, published in 1946, one of the characters is described by another as "a [Whitechapel](/wiki/Whitechapel "Whitechapel") Jewess with dyed hair and a voice like a [corncrake](/wiki/Corncrake "Corncrake") ... a small woman with a thick nose, henna red hair and a disagreeable voice". The idea that Shinichi Kudo would be turned into a child stemmed from the idea of a [Tortoiseshell cat](/wiki/Tortoiseshell_cat "Tortoiseshell cat") [Sherlock Holmes](/wiki/Sherlock_Holmes "Sherlock Holmes") as a protagonist.[[6]](#cite_note-Fami_2011-8) [Gosho Aoyama](/wiki/Gosho_Aoyama "Gosho Aoyama")'s idea was the cat would indicate the crucial evidence needed to solve the case; a performance the child-turned Shinichi does to help those around with the investigation. Shinichi was inspired by the fictional private eye Shunsaku Kudo, the protagonist of the Japanese television series [Tantei Monogatari](/wiki/Tantei_Monogatari "Tantei Monogatari"). [[7]](#cite_note-9) Aoyama revealed that his editor was against the name Conan due to the protagonist from the anime series *[Future Boy Conan](/wiki/Future_Boy_Conan "Future Boy Conan")* sharing the same name and had suggested to name him Doyle instead. The author stuck with the name Conan believing it would overtake the *Future Boy* series. According to Aoyama, Shinichi's catch phrase, "There is always only one truth!" (真実はいつもひとつ!, *Shinjitsu wa Itsumo Hitotsu!*), was thought of by the [anime](/wiki/Anime "Anime") adaptation's script writer and written into chapter 95 of the manga at the same time.[[6]](#cite_note-Fami_2011-8) In the English localizations, the catch phrase is translated as "One Truth Prevails".[[8]](#cite_note-10)[[9]](#cite_note-11)

Aoyama said that it took him only a single minute to come up with Conan's design.[[10]](#cite_note-bonus83-12) The character's basic hairstyle is similar to that of the protagonist of his previous series *[Yaiba](/wiki/Yaiba "Yaiba")*, only "silkier", while the [cowlick](/wiki/Cowlick "Cowlick") was inspired by Kabu from *[Sally the Witch](/wiki/Sally_the_Witch "Sally the Witch")*. Cabernet Franc :: Wine regions :: chunk_0003
Across the world Cabernet Franc is one of the twenty most widely planted [grape varieties](/wiki/Grape_varieties "Grape varieties"). Plantings are found throughout Europe, in the [New World](/wiki/New_World_(wine) "New World (wine)"), [China](/wiki/China_(wine) "China (wine)") and [Kazakhstan](/wiki/Kazakhstan_(wine) "Kazakhstan (wine)"). In many regions, it is planted as a component of a Bordeaux-style blend such as [Meritage](/wiki/Meritage "Meritage"), playing secondary role to Cabernet Sauvignon and [Merlot](/wiki/Merlot "Merlot"). In parts of northeast [Italy](/wiki/Italy_(wine) "Italy (wine)"), [Anjou](/wiki/Anjou_(wine) "Anjou (wine)")-[Saumur](/wiki/Saumur_(wine) "Saumur (wine)"), [Touraine](/wiki/Touraine "Touraine") and the [right bank](/wiki/Right_bank_(wine) "Right bank (wine)") region of Bordeaux, Cabernet Franc both plays a more prominent role in blends and is vinted as a [varietal](/wiki/Varietal "Varietal").[[4]](#cite_note-Oxford_pg_118-119-4)

Astro (South Korean band) :: Career :: 2020: One & Only, Gateway, and first sub-unit Moonbin & Sanha :: chunk_0005
On February 14, 2020, Moonbin appeared in a [V Live](/wiki/V_Live "V Live") broadcast with the other Astro members, officially ending his hiatus.[[68]](#cite_note-68) In celebration of their fourth debut anniversary, Astro released a special digital single album titled *[One & Only](/wiki/One_%26_Only_(Astro_song) "One & Only (Astro song)")* on February 23.[[69]](#cite_note-69) A physical edition of the single was released on March 13.[[70]](#cite_note-70)

In May 4, Astro released their seventh extended play *[Gateway](/wiki/Gateway_(EP) "Gateway (EP)")*.[[71]](#cite_note-71) On May 12, the EP's lead single "Knock" earned the group their second win on the [MBC M](/wiki/MBC_M "MBC M") music show *[Show Champion](/wiki/Show_Champion "Show Champion")*.[[72]](#cite_note-72) On June 28, Astro held their first online live streaming concert 2020 Astro Live on WWW, where they performed the song "No, I Don't" for the first time.[[73]](#cite_note-73) On the same day, the single was distributed digitally through various streaming services.[[74]](#cite_note-74)

On August 14, [Fantagio](/wiki/Fantagio "Fantagio") confirmed that members Moonbin and [Yoon San-ha](/wiki/Yoon_San-ha "Yoon San-ha") would form Astro's first sub-unit called [Moonbin & Sanha](/wiki/Moonbin_%26_Sanha "Moonbin & Sanha") and that the recording for the unit's first [extended play](/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") had already been completed.[[75]](#cite_note-75) Their debut EP *In-Out*, featuring the lead single "Bad Idea", was released on September 14.[[76]](#cite_note-76)[[77]](#cite_note-77) Eight days later, on September 22, the sub-unit received their first music show award from *[The Show](/wiki/The_Show_(South_Korean_TV_program) "The Show (South Korean TV program)")*, making them the fastest K-pop sub-unit to receive their first win on a music show.[[78]](#cite_note-78)

Germany :: Politics :: Constituent states :: chunk_0015
Main articles: [States of Germany](/wiki/States_of_Germany "States of Germany"), [Federalism in Germany](/wiki/Federalism_in_Germany "Federalism in Germany"), and [List of current heads of government of the German federal states](/wiki/List_of_current_heads_of_government_of_the_German_federal_states "List of current heads of government of the German federal states")

Germany is a [federation](/wiki/Federation "Federation") comprising sixteen constituent states referred to as *Länder*,[[135]](#cite_note-Britannica-140) thirteen of which are so-called "area-states" (*Flächenländer*). Two states, [Berlin](/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and [Hamburg](/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), are [city-states](/wiki/Independent_city#Stadtstaaten "Independent city") (*Stadtstaaten*), in which there is no separation between state government and local administration. The state of [Bremen](/wiki/Bremen_(state) "Bremen (state)"), though officially also called a *Stadtstaat*, consists of the cities of [Bremen](/wiki/Bremen_(city) "Bremen (city)"), for which the state government also serves as the municipal administration, and the exclave of [Bremerhaven](/wiki/Bremerhaven "Bremerhaven").[[136]](#cite_note-141)

Each state (*Land*) has its own constitution[[137]](#cite_note-142) and is largely autonomous in its organisation.[[135]](#cite_note-Britannica-140) As of 2017, Germany is divided into 401 [districts](/wiki/Districts_of_Germany "Districts of Germany") (*Kreise*) at a municipal level; these consist of 294 [rural districts](/wiki/List_of_rural_districts_of_Germany "List of rural districts of Germany") and 107 [urban districts](/wiki/Urban_districts_of_Germany "Urban districts of Germany").[[138]](#cite_note-143)
